intro: A woman sits at an open window for one hour and whispers a word she is not supposed to feel. A walker stands where two roads split and, years later, tells a story about it that the poem quietly contradicts. A man stands over a dead body in a Roman square and, without accusing anyone, turns a city into a mob. Three pages, twenty lines, one scene. Each is small, and each holds more than most whole books.

This unit is about reading small things slowly. Fiction first: what a story says, how it says it, why the writer chose every word, and how characters, structure and point of view carry a theme. Then poetry: line breaks, meter, sound, image, speaker, tone and the turn where a poem changes its mind. Then drama: acts and scenes, soliloquy and aside, Shakespeare's language decoded, tragedy's shape, and what happens to a scene when someone stands up and plays it.

By the end you will be able to take a paragraph, a stanza or a speech, say exactly what it does, point to the words that do it, and explain why it matters, in writing that someone could argue with. That skill is called close reading. It works on Chopin and Shakespeare, and it works on a text message, a contract and a campaign ad. It is the difference between being told what a text means and finding out for yourself.
bigQuestion: How do writers make a few chosen words carry meaning that a reader can find, prove and argue about?

timeline.t: Shakespeare's Romeo and Juliet: a prologue tells the ending before the play begins.
Julius Caesar: Brutus speaks in prose, Antony in verse, and the crowd turns.
Macbeth sees a dagger in the air, alone on stage, and tells the audience the truth.
Shakespeare's sonnets are published: fourteen lines, three quatrains, a couplet, a turn.
Poe's narrator in The Tell-Tale Heart insists he is sane while proving otherwise.
Whitman's Song of Myself throws out meter and builds an I large enough for everyone.
Dickinson writes that hope is the thing with feathers; the poems stay in a drawer until after her death.
Gilman's The Yellow Wallpaper: a woman under the rest cure writes a journal she must hide.
Chopin's The Story of an Hour: one hour, an open window, and a word whispered three times.
Dunbar's We Wear the Mask gives smooth rhyme to hidden pain.
Crane's The Open Boat: four men row toward a shore that never gets closer.
Frost's The Road Not Taken: two roads, worn about the same, and a sigh in the future.

words.d: reading a text slowly to see what it says, how it says it, and why the writer chose it
a writer's choice of words
a character with conflicting wants who develops over a story
a narrator whose account the reader has reason to doubt
an idea about life that a text develops, stated as a full sentence
the speed at which a story moves through its events
a ten-syllable line of five soft-loud pairs, the meter of Shakespeare's sonnets and plays
the voice that says a poem's words, created by the poet
the point where a poem changes direction, tone or meaning; the volta
a speech by a character alone on stage that reveals true thoughts
when the audience knows something a character does not
the weakness in a character that leads to their downfall

test.q: What is the first step of close reading?
choices: Deciding the theme
Stating the literal facts of what the text says
Finding the rhyme scheme
Comparing the text to a film
test.why: Close reading starts from what the text says, then moves to how and why.

test.q: Why does Louise Mallard's death feel like a loss of freedom rather than joy to a reader?
choices: Because the doctors say so
Because Brently was cruel
Because the reader saw her at the window whispering free, and the doctors did not
Because the story is set in winter
test.why: The reader holds knowledge the doctors lack; the spring images and the whispered word teach us to read her death as a life cut off.

test.q: Which sentence states a theme rather than a topic?
choices: Marriage
The Story of an Hour
Freedom
Even a kind marriage can feel like a loss of self
test.why: A theme is a full-sentence idea about life; the others are topics or a title.

test.q: Poe's narrator in The Tell-Tale Heart is called unreliable because
choices: he never gives his name
he insists he is sane while describing acts that prove he is not
he tells the story out of order
he is a minor character
test.why: The gap between what he claims and what he shows gives the reader reason to doubt him.

test.q: What does cultural context add to reading The Yellow Wallpaper?
choices: Knowing the rest cure was a real treatment that harmed women changes how we see the husband
It proves the wallpaper was haunted
It shows the narrator was lazy
It tells us the story is a comedy
test.why: Context turns the husband's gentle orders into part of a confining medical practice.

test.q: What does Crane gain by repeating the rowing in The Open Boat?
choices: A faster plot
The reader feels the men's exhaustion and the sea's indifference
Proof that the captain is brave
A happy ending
test.why: Structural repetition makes the reader share the men's tired dread.

test.q: What do the middle stanzas of Frost's The Road Not Taken say about the two roads?
choices: One was clearly less traveled
One led to a city
They were worn about the same
One was closed
test.why: The poem admits the roads were really about the same before the ending claims otherwise.

test.q: A line of ten syllables in five soft-loud pairs is
choices: free verse
a quatrain
slant rhyme
iambic pentameter

test.q: Why should analysis of a poem say speaker rather than poet?
choices: Because the voice in a poem is a created character, not necessarily the author
Because poets prefer it
Because it makes the essay longer
Because poems never use I
test.why: The speaker is built by the poet, like a narrator, and may differ from the author entirely.

test.q: Where is the turn in Shakespeare's Sonnet 18?
choices: The first line
Line nine, beginning with but
The title
There is no turn
test.why: After eight lines on summer's flaws, line nine turns to the beloved's eternal summer.

test.q: What should you do before writing an analysis of a poem?
choices: Memorize it
Find the poet's biography
Paraphrase it in plain prose
Count its words
test.why: Paraphrasing first makes sure you know what the poem literally says.

test.q: Why does Antony win the crowd that Brutus just persuaded?
choices: He speaks in prose
He accuses Brutus directly
He is Caesar's son
He uses questions, repetition, the body and the will while never openly accusing anyone
test.why: Antony's rhetoric turns the word honorable inside out and puts Caesar's wounds in front of the crowd.

test.q: Which is an example of dramatic irony?
choices: Romeo grieving over Juliet while the audience knows she is only drugged
Antony calling Brutus honorable
Macbeth speaking to a dagger
Brutus choosing prose
test.why: Dramatic irony is the audience knowing what a character does not.

test.q: What makes Macbeth's fall a tragedy rather than bad luck?
choices: The witches force him
He is killed in battle
His fall comes from his own choice, driven by ambition
His wife dies
test.why: Tragedy requires a downfall caused by the character's own flaw and action.

test.q: Two actors deliver the same line with different pace and eye contact and create two different characters. What does this show?
choices: One actor made a mistake
The script is unfinished
The line has no meaning
A script leaves performance choices open, and those choices shape meaning
test.why: Delivery, movement and pause are decisions the text leaves to a production.

write.prompt: Choose one text from this unit: The Story of an Hour, The Road Not Taken, or Antony's funeral speech. Make a claim about how one specific choice by the writer (a repeated word, a structure, a point of view, a turn) shapes what the reader or audience understands. Support it with quoted or precisely described evidence and explain your reasoning.
tips: Claim: name the technique and its effect in one sentence someone could argue against, such as 'Frost's future tense turns a coin flip into a story of courage.'
Evidence: quote the smallest piece that proves your point, embedded in your own sentence, or describe the exact moment.
Reasoning: after every quotation, write at least one sentence explaining what the words do to the reader.
The other side: state the common reading (the doctors' joy, the brave road, the honest Brutus) and show what in the text it misses.
Say speaker or narrator, not poet or author, unless the text clearly speaks as its writer.

title: Literature: Close Reading

chapters.title: Fiction
chapters.bigQuestion: How does a short story make a reader feel something with only a few pages of carefully chosen words?

story.title: One Hour in a Closed Room
story.kicker: A woman is told her husband died in a train wreck. Sixty minutes later, the front door opens.
paragraphs: In 1894 Kate Chopin published a story that fits on three pages. It begins with a warning: Louise Mallard has a weak heart, so the news must be broken gently. Her sister Josephine tells her, in broken sentences, that her husband Brently has died in a railroad accident. Louise weeps at once, wildly, in her sister's arms. Then she goes upstairs alone, shuts the door of her room, and sinks into a chair by an open window.

Here the story slows down. Outside the window it is spring. Trees shake with new leaves. Someone is singing far off, and sparrows twitter in the eaves. Patches of blue sky show between the clouds. Louise sits very still. Something is coming toward her, she feels, out of the sky and the sounds and the smell of rain. She is afraid of it. She tries to push it back. Then she stops trying, and a word slips out of her lips, whispered over and over. The word is free.

Chopin does not tell us that Louise hated her husband. She tells us the opposite: he was kind, he loved her, and she had sometimes loved him. What Louise sees, in that chair, is the long line of years ahead that will belong to her alone. No one will bend her will to theirs. She prays for a long life, and only yesterday she had shuddered at the thought of a long life. Josephine kneels outside the locked door, begging her to open it. Louise finally rises, and the story says she walks out of the room like a goddess of victory.

At the bottom of the stairs, a key turns in the lock. Brently Mallard walks in, holding his umbrella, a little dusty from travel. He had been nowhere near the accident. He had not even known there was one. Josephine screams. Louise's heart stops. The last sentence of the story reports what the doctors said: she died of heart disease, of joy that kills.

Read fast, the story is a twist ending. Read slowly, sentence by sentence, it is something stranger and sadder. The doctors are wrong about the joy, and the reader is the only person in the house who knows it. This chapter is about reading that slowly: what a story says, how it says it, and why a writer might choose every one of those words.
story.think: The doctors say Louise died of joy. What do you think killed her, and what sentence in the story would you point to?

lessons.title: What the Text Says
lessons.mainIdea: Close reading starts with the plain facts of the text: who, what, where, and in what order, before any interpretation.
reading: Read this sentence from a story written for this lesson: "Marcus set the letter on the table, unopened, and went out to shovel the walk for the third time that morning." Before you decide what it means, get the facts straight. A man named Marcus has a letter. He does not open it. He goes outside to shovel snow. He has already shoveled twice today. Those are the things the sentence says. Everything else is something you add.

This first step is called reading for what the text *says*. It sounds too easy to bother with, and that is exactly why readers skip it and go wrong. A reader who is moving fast might remember that Marcus "threw the letter away" or "read the letter and got upset." The sentence says neither. When you analyze a story, every claim you make has to rest on what is actually on the page. If you start from a misreading, every conclusion after it is built on sand.

A useful habit is to *summarize* a passage in one or two plain sentences, with no opinion in them. For the story of Louise Mallard, a fair summary would be: a woman with a heart condition is told her husband died; alone in her room she feels a rush of freedom; her husband walks in alive, and she dies. Notice what the summary leaves out. It does not say she was glad, or that she was a bad wife, or that the ending is ironic. Those ideas may be true, but they are the next step, not the first one.

Try it now with a longer piece. When you read any story in this chapter, pause after each page and ask three flat questions. Who is here? What just happened? What has changed since the last page? Write the answers in a margin or a notebook. You will be surprised how often the answer to the third question is the key to the whole story, and how often a reader who did not stop to ask it misses the point.

words.d: in close reading, the literal facts a text states, before any interpretation
to retell the main events or ideas of a text briefly and without adding opinion
a reader's explanation of what a text means, built on what it says

look.title: The First Sentence
look.text: Knowing that Mrs. Mallard was afflicted with a heart trouble, great care was taken to break to her as gently as possible the news of her husband's death.
look.cite: Kate Chopin, The Story of an Hour, 1894
look.prompt: List every fact this one sentence gives you. Which of those facts turns out to matter at the very end of the story?

check.q: What does it mean to read for what a text says?
choices: To decide what the author's hidden message is
To state the literal facts of the text before interpreting
To guess how the story will end
To find the most beautiful sentence
check.why: Reading for what the text says means getting the plain facts straight first. Interpretation comes after.

check.q: In the model sentence, what does Marcus actually do with the letter?
choices: He reads it and gets upset
He throws it away
He sets it on the table unopened
He mails it
check.why: The sentence says he set it on the table, unopened. The other answers add things the text never says.

check.q: Why should a summary leave out words like "glad" or "ironic"?
choices: Because those ideas are interpretations, not facts stated by the text
Because summaries must be under ten words
Because stories never include feelings
Because those words are too hard for readers
check.why: A summary states what happens. Whether Louise was glad or the ending is ironic is a judgment the reader makes afterward.

lessons.title: How the Text Says It
lessons.mainIdea: Once you know what a passage says, look at how it says it: word choice, sentence length, images, and what is repeated or left out.
reading: Here are two sentences that say the same thing. First: "She was very sad when she heard the news." Second: "She wept at once, with sudden, wild abandonment, in her sister's arms." The second is close to how Chopin describes Louise Mallard's first reaction. Both report grief. But the second one has a body in it. It has arms and a sudden storm of crying, and it has the word wild. The choice of those words is the *how* of the sentence, and it is where a story's meaning actually lives.

Close readers look at four things when they study how a text says something. First, *diction*, which means word choice: why wild and not sad? Second, sentence length and rhythm: is the sentence short and blunt, or long and winding? Third, images, the pictures a sentence puts in your mind: open window, new leaves, patches of blue sky. Fourth, patterns: what word or idea comes back again and again, and what is oddly missing. In Chopin's story, the word free is whispered three times in a row, and the husband's name barely appears while Louise sits at the window.

Look at this passage written for this lesson: "The kitchen was clean. The counters were clean. The floor, which she had mopped twice, was clean. Nobody had eaten anything in that house for two days." What the passage says is simple: a clean kitchen, no eating. How it says it is the point. The word clean lands three times like a hammer. The sentences are short and flat. The last sentence explains the first three without saying the word grief once. A reader who notices the repetition and the flatness understands the character better than any label could tell them.

When you write about a story, the how is your evidence. "Louise is happy" is a claim. "Chopin describes the sky outside her window as showing patches of blue and has her whisper the word free three times" is evidence for the claim. Practice moving from one to the other. Underline one striking word in a paragraph, and ask what would change if the writer had picked a plainer one.

words.d: a writer's choice of words, such as wild instead of sad
a word picture that appeals to the senses, such as new leaves shaking in spring
something a text repeats or arranges on purpose, such as a word used three times
specific words, sentences or details from the text that support a claim

look.title: Same Fact, Two Ways
look.text: Two writers describe the same moment, a boy finding out his family is moving. Writer A: "He was upset about the move." Writer B: "He kept nodding while his father talked, and afterward he could not remember a single word, only the sound of the tape gun sealing the first box in the hall."
look.prompt: What does Writer B's version tell you about the boy that Writer A's does not? Point to one word or image.

check.q: What does the term diction mean?
choices: The order of events in a story
The lesson a story teaches
How a text is divided into chapters
A writer's choice of words
check.why: Diction is word choice. Choosing wild instead of sad is a matter of diction.

check.q: In the model kitchen passage, what does repeating the word clean three times do?
choices: It shows the character loves housework
It shows the character is coping with grief by scrubbing and not eating
It proves the house is for sale
It has no effect; it is just careless writing
check.why: The repetition, the flat sentences and the last line about nobody eating together suggest grief without naming it.

check.q: Which of these is evidence rather than a claim?
choices: Louise feels a rush of freedom
The story has a sad ending
Chopin was a great writer
Chopin has Louise whisper the word free three times
check.why: Evidence points to specific words on the page. The other three are judgments a reader makes about the text.

lessons.title: Why the Writer Chose It
lessons.mainIdea: The last step of close reading asks why: what effect does a choice have on the reader, and what would be lost if the writer had done it differently?
reading: Chopin could have opened her story with the train wreck. Smoke, screaming, a list of the dead. Instead she opens in a quiet house with a sentence about a woman's weak heart. Why? Ask what the choice does. It makes the reader nervous for Louise before anything happens. It keeps our attention on her body and her feelings, not on the accident. And it plants the fact the last sentence will need. A writer's choice is never just decoration. It sets up an *effect*, a change in what the reader knows, feels or expects.

The question why is the hardest of the three, and it is where students most often freeze. Here is a way in. Take the choice you noticed and imagine the *alternative*, the thing the writer could have done instead. Then compare. Suppose Chopin had let Louise sit at a window facing a brick wall on a gray day. The word free would still be whispered, but it would sound like madness. With spring outside the window, it sounds like the world agreeing with her. The alternative shows you what the actual choice is doing.

Read this pair written for this lesson. Version one: "Dad came home at six. He said he lost his job. We ate dinner." Version two: "Dad came home at six, like always, and set his lunchbox on the counter, like always, and told us the plant was closing, and then he asked what was for dinner." Why does version two keep saying like always? Because the writer wants the reader to feel the ordinary evening cracking. The bad news arrives inside a routine that has not yet noticed it is over. Version one reports the same events and produces almost nothing.

When you write the why, use verbs that name an effect: the choice builds suspense, softens a blow, makes us trust a character, makes us doubt one, delays the truth. Then finish with what the reader ends up believing or feeling that they would not have otherwise. Says, how, why: that is close reading, and it works on a paragraph, a page or a whole book.

words.d: the change a writer's choice produces in what the reader knows, feels or expects
what a writer could have done instead; comparing it shows what the real choice does
reading a text slowly to see what it says, how it says it, and why

look.title: The Umbrella
look.text: When Brently Mallard walks in alive at the end of Chopin's story, he is carrying his umbrella and a travel bag, and he is a little dusty from the trip. The story could have simply said that he walked in. Instead it gives us these small, ordinary objects.
look.prompt: Why give him an umbrella? What effect do these ordinary details have at the moment Louise's world collapses a second time?

check.q: What is the best way to figure out why a writer made a choice?
choices: Look up what critics say about the author
Imagine what the writer could have done instead and compare the effects
Count the number of words in the passage
Assume every choice is meant to be beautiful
check.why: Comparing the real choice to an alternative shows what the choice does that the alternative would not.

check.q: Why does Chopin open with Louise's weak heart instead of the train wreck?
choices: Because train wrecks were not allowed in stories in 1894
Because she forgot to describe the wreck
It makes us worried for Louise and plants a fact the ending needs
It shows the story is really about medicine
check.why: The opening keeps attention on Louise and sets up the last sentence about her heart.

check.q: In the model passage, what effect does repeating like always have?
choices: It makes the reader feel an ordinary evening cracking under bad news
It shows the family is bored
It makes the passage easier to read aloud
It proves the father is lying
check.why: The routine phrase makes the news feel like it is breaking into a normal night that has not noticed it is over.

lessons.title: Complex Characters
lessons.mainIdea: A complex character wants more than one thing, changes across the story, and cannot be summed up in one word.
reading: Think of a character from a cartoon you watched as a small child. The villain wanted to be bad. The hero wanted to be good. You could describe each one in a single word, and nothing they did ever surprised you. That is a *flat character*. Now think of a person you actually know: a friend who is generous and also jealous, a parent who is strict because they are afraid. Real people hold contradictions. Fiction that feels true builds characters the same way, and we call them *complex characters* or round characters.

Louise Mallard is complex. She loved her husband sometimes. She weeps real tears when she hears he is dead. And within the hour she is whispering that she is free. None of these cancels the others out. Chopin even tells us that Louise knows she will weep again when she sees his kind hands folded in death. A flat version of Louise would be a cold wife who is glad, or a devoted wife who is destroyed. The real Louise is both grieving and glad, and the story's power comes from holding those two things in one body at one window.

Here is a short model written for this lesson. "Tasha had told her little brother she would come to his game. She had also told her manager she would take the extra shift, because rent was due Friday. At four o'clock she stood in the break room with her coat half on, listening to the clock." Tasha is not lazy or selfish; she is pulled. A reader who watches her stand there with her coat half on knows more about her than any list of traits could say.

To analyze a complex character, do not stop at one adjective. Track the character across the story and ask: what does this person want, what else do they want, and where do those wants collide? Then look for the moment of change, the place where they act differently than they would have on page one. Complex characters develop, and tracing that development is one of the main things a close reader does.

words.d: a character with one trait who does not change, like a cartoon villain
a character with mixed traits and conflicting wants who develops over a story; also called round
to change or grow over the course of a story

look.title: One Word Is Not Enough
look.text: A student writes, "Louise Mallard is a selfish character." Her partner points to the paragraph where Louise cries in her sister's arms, and to the line where the story says she knows she will weep again over her husband's kind hands. The first student crosses out selfish and writes two words instead.
look.prompt: What two words might she write, and why does the story need both of them?

check.q: Which of these best describes a complex character?
choices: A character who is always the villain
A character described in one word who never changes
A character who has a lot of lines of dialogue
A character with conflicting wants who develops during the story
check.why: Complex characters hold contradictions and change. Flat characters have one trait and stay the same.

check.q: What makes Louise Mallard complex rather than flat?
choices: She has a heart condition
She both grieves her husband and feels free without him
She lives in a big house
She never speaks in the story
check.why: Louise weeps real tears and also whispers free. Holding both at once is what makes her complex.

check.q: In the model text, what does Tasha standing with her coat half on show?
choices: She is pulled between two promises she made
She is cold
She has decided to quit her job
She forgot about the game
check.why: Her coat is half on because she is caught between her brother's game and the shift that pays rent.

lessons.title: Conflicting Motivations
lessons.mainIdea: Motivation is the reason a character acts; when two motivations pull in opposite directions, the story's conflict often lives inside one person.
reading: In Edgar Allan Poe's story "The Tell-Tale Heart," published in 1843, a man insists that he is not mad, then explains how he murdered an old man because of the old man's pale blue eye. He says he loved the old man. He says the old man had never wronged him. And still he creeps into his room every night for a week. The narrator's *motivation*, the reason behind his actions, is the puzzle at the center of the story. He claims one thing and does another, and the gap between them is where a reader has to work.

Most great stories put opposing motivations inside a single character. In Nathaniel Hawthorne's "Young Goodman Brown," from 1835, a young husband leaves his wife at sunset to keep a mysterious appointment in the forest. He wants to go; he also feels he should turn back, and he says so several times. He keeps walking. What he finds in the forest, or dreams he finds, ruins the rest of his life. The story never settles whether the night was real, but the conflict between his curiosity and his conscience is real on every page.

Here is a model written for this lesson. "Jamal wanted to tell the coach who had broken the window. He also wanted to be the kind of person who did not tell. He sat in the locker room after everyone left, tying and untying the same shoe." Notice that the writer never uses the word torn. The shoe does the work. When you read for motivation, watch what characters do with their hands, where they linger, and what they say twice. Those are the places where two motives are fighting.

To write about conflicting motivations, name both pulls and then point to the moment one wins. Louise Mallard's love for her husband pulls one way; her hunger for a life of her own pulls the other. At the window, the second wins, and Chopin marks it with the whispered word. Later, at the bottom of the stairs, the story does not tell us which feeling stops her heart. That silence is a choice too, and a close reader notices it.

words.d: the reason behind a character's actions and choices
the struggle that drives a story; it can be between characters or inside one character
the voice that tells the story, which may or may not be trustworthy

look.title: A Narrator Who Protests
look.text: True!—nervous—very, very dreadfully nervous I had been and am; but why will you say that I am mad?
look.cite: Edgar Allan Poe, The Tell-Tale Heart, 1843
look.prompt: The narrator opens by denying he is mad before anyone has accused him. What does that tell you about his motivation for telling the story at all?

check.q: What is a character's motivation?
choices: The reason behind the character's actions
The character's name and age
The setting the character lives in
The number of scenes the character appears in
check.why: Motivation is the why behind what a character does.

check.q: What conflict pulls at Young Goodman Brown as he walks into the forest?
choices: Hunger against thirst
His curiosity against his conscience
His wife against his mother
Fear of the dark against fear of the light
check.why: He wants to keep his appointment and also feels he should turn back, and says so several times while walking on.

check.q: In the Jamal model, how does the writer show conflicting motivations?
choices: By saying Jamal is torn
By having the coach ask him directly
By describing the broken window
Through a repeated action, tying and untying the same shoe
check.why: The writer never says torn. The repeated small action shows the two motives fighting.

lessons.title: Point of View
lessons.mainIdea: Who tells the story, and how much they know, shapes everything the reader is allowed to see.
reading: Charlotte Perkins Gilman's "The Yellow Wallpaper," from 1892, is told by a woman writing in a secret journal. Her husband, a doctor, has confined her to an upstairs room to rest after the birth of her baby. He forbids her to write. She writes anyway, in short entries, and over weeks she becomes convinced that a woman is trapped behind the pattern of the room's yellow wallpaper. The reader never gets the husband's side. We see only what the narrator sees, and by the end we are watching her mind come apart from the inside. That is the power of *first-person* point of view.

Point of view is the position from which a story is told. In first person, a character tells it using I, and we know only what that character knows or admits. In *third-person limited*, a narrator outside the story uses he or she but stays inside one character's head; Chopin's story stays close to Louise this way. In *third-person omniscient*, the narrator knows everything about everyone and may move from mind to mind. Each choice trades something. First person gives intimacy but takes away certainty. Omniscient gives certainty but can feel distant.

A narrator can also be *unreliable*, meaning the reader has reason to doubt what they say. Poe's murderer in "The Tell-Tale Heart" says he is calm and sane while describing a crime that proves the opposite. Gilman's narrator reports the wallpaper moving. The story never announces that these narrators are wrong. It leaves clues, such as facts that do not add up or feelings the narrator denies too loudly, and trusts the reader to see around the narrator's shoulder.

Read this model written for this lesson: "I did not take the money. I want that clear. I was in the office, yes, and the drawer was open, and I looked, because anyone would look. But I left with the same twenty dollars I came in with, and the fact that nobody believes me is their problem." What point of view is this? First person. Is the narrator reliable? Watch the sentence about the twenty dollars. A close reader hears a defense that has been rehearsed.

words.d: the position from which a story is told, such as first person or third person
narration by a character in the story using I
narration from outside the story that stays inside one character's mind
a narrator whose account the reader has reason to doubt

look.title: A Journal No One Is Supposed to See
look.text: The narrator of Gilman's story writes that her husband, a physician, does not believe she is sick, and that she must hide her journal because he has told her that writing will make her worse. She describes the wallpaper as a color that revolts her and a pattern that seems to change as she watches it.
look.cite: Charlotte Perkins Gilman, The Yellow Wallpaper, 1892 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: The narrator is sure the pattern moves. The reader cannot check. How does telling the story in first person make the wallpaper more frightening?

check.q: In which point of view does the reader know only what a character telling the story in I knows?

lessons.title: Cultural Context
lessons.mainIdea: Knowing when and where a story was written helps you see what its characters could and could not do, and why the writer's choices were bold.
reading: Why does Louise Mallard whisper free instead of shouting it? Part of the answer is the year: 1894. A married woman in most of the United States then had few legal rights of her own. She could rarely sign a contract, keep her own wages, or vote. Divorce was a scandal. Chopin's readers would have understood, without being told, that Louise's only door to a life of her own was the one death had just opened. The story's *cultural context*, the time, place and beliefs around it, is the air the characters breathe.

Context also explains "The Yellow Wallpaper." Gilman's narrator is being treated with a real medical fashion of the 1880s called the rest cure. Doctors told women with nervous illness to lie still, avoid work, and stop thinking. Gilman herself was given this treatment and later wrote that it nearly destroyed her. Knowing that, the husband's gentle orders in the story stop sounding like care and start sounding like a cage. A reader who does not know the context may blame the narrator. A reader who knows it understands the room.

Context is not an excuse to stop reading the text. It is a tool for reading it better. Here is a model written for this lesson: "Her grandmother had never learned to read, and she signed her name with an X on the day the deed was recorded. My mother framed that page." Without context, this is a family scrapbook. With the fact that reading was once forbidden to many enslaved people in this country, the framed X becomes something else: proof of a history and a claim on the land in the same mark.

When you read older fiction, ask two context questions. What could this character do in this time and place, and what could they not? And what did the writer risk by writing this? Chopin's stories about women's inner lives drew criticism in her own day. Reading with context lets you see that a quiet story of one hour in a closed room was, in its moment, a daring thing to publish.

lessons.title: Theme Built From Details
lessons.mainIdea: A theme is an idea about life that a story develops; you find it by tracing how specific details keep pointing the same way.
reading: Ask a class what "The Story of an Hour" is about and someone will say "a woman whose husband dies." That is the topic. A *theme* is different. A theme is what the story says about its topic, an idea about life that could be true outside the story too. One theme of Chopin's story might be that even a loving marriage can feel like a loss of self. Notice that a theme is a full sentence, not a single word. "Freedom" is a topic. "Freedom can be more frightening than grief" is a theme.

You do not find a theme by guessing. You find it by watching details pile up in one direction. In Chopin's story, the window is open. The trees are full of new spring life. The sky shows blue. Louise's pulse beats fast and warms her body. Every detail in that room points toward life beginning, not ending. Then the story ends with a death that the doctors call joy. Put the pattern of details next to that ending, and a theme starts to take shape: the life Louise glimpsed was real, and losing it is what killed her.

Details also *refine* a theme, which means they make it sharper and more specific. Early in the story you might think the theme is simply that Louise wanted to be free. Then Chopin adds that her husband was kind, that his face had only ever looked on her with love. That detail refines the idea. The story is not about escaping a cruel man. It is about how even kindness, when it comes with the power to bend another person's will, can be a kind of prison. The added detail makes the theme both truer and harder.

Here is a model written for this lesson. "Every morning Ana's father drove her to school, past the bus stop where her friends stood laughing. He said the bus was not safe. He said it the way he said everything: gently, finally." One detail, gently, finally, refines the whole picture. The father is loving, and the love has a lock on it. When you write about theme, trace the details in order and show how each one adjusts the idea.

what a story is about on the surface, such as marriage or freedom
to make an idea sharper and more specific as new details are added

lessons.title: Order and Pacing
lessons.mainIdea: Writers control the order in which events are told and how fast they move, and both choices shape what the reader feels.
reading: Chopin's story covers one hour, but the story does not treat every minute the same. The news arrives in a few sentences. The husband's return takes a paragraph. The stretch in between, Louise alone at the window, takes up most of the story's length. Time stretches when the writer slows down to look closely, and it snaps shut when the writer hurries. This control of speed is called *pacing*, and it is one of the most powerful tools a storyteller has.

Order is the other tool. Most stories move in *chronological order*, from first event to last. But a writer can start in the middle and go back, a move called *flashback*, or hint at what is coming, called *foreshadowing*. Poe's narrator in "The Tell-Tale Heart" tells his story after the crime, so we know from the first line that something terrible happened, and we read to find out how. The first sentence of Chopin's story foreshadows the last one: a weak heart, mentioned before anything else, is the fact the ending will turn on.

Here is a model written for this lesson, two versions of the same moment. Slow: "The envelope was thin. She turned it over. Her name was spelled right, which was rare. She slid a finger under the flap and stopped, and looked at the ceiling, and then she opened it." Fast: "She tore it open. Rejected." The slow version makes the reader wait with her, and the waiting is the emotion. The fast version is a slap. Neither is better; they do different jobs, and a good writer picks the speed that fits the moment.

When you analyze pacing and order, ask where the story spends its words and why. Which scene is told slowly, and what does the slowness let you notice? Which is told in a rush, and what does the rush hide or sharpen? If a story steps out of time order, ask what the reader learns early or late because of it. Structure is a set of choices about time, and every one of them has an effect.

words.d: the speed at which a story moves through events, slow in some places and fast in others
telling events in the order they happened
a scene that goes back to an earlier time than the main story
a hint early in a story about something that will happen later

The setting of a story

Foreshadowing

lessons.title: Parallel Plots and Pattern
lessons.mainIdea: Some stories run two lines of action side by side, or repeat a pattern, so that one part comments on another.
reading: Stephen Crane's "The Open Boat," published in 1897, puts four men in a tiny lifeboat after a shipwreck: a captain, a cook, an oiler, and a correspondent. For most of the story they row toward a shore they can see but cannot reach. Crane builds the story out of repetition. The men row, they trade places, they see the shore, they get no closer. The same phrases return. The repetition is the point: the sea does not care about them, and the story's *structure*, its shape, makes the reader feel that indifference in their own tired arms.

Crane based the story on something that happened to him. In January 1897 the ship he was on sank off the coast of Florida. He spent about thirty hours in a small boat before reaching land. Knowing that does not tell you what the story means, but it explains why the details feel so exact: the way a wave looks from below, the way an oar blisters the hands. Close reading of structure asks what the repeated parts have in common and what changes, if anything, from one repetition to the next.

A second structural choice is the *parallel plot*, two story lines that run beside each other and reflect one another. Here is a model written for this lesson. "On the third floor, Mr. Reyes graded essays until the building went dark. On the first floor, the custodian's daughter did her homework at a folding table while her mother mopped the hall, and when the lights went out she kept writing by the glow of her phone." Nothing connects these two people except the building and the dark. Placing them side by side makes each one say something about the other.

When you meet a story with two threads, ask what the writer gains by refusing to tell just one. Usually the answer is contrast, or an echo: the same problem faced by two people, or the same night lived two ways. When you meet repetition, ask what it makes you feel. In Crane's boat the repetition is exhaustion and dread. In a comedy the same device might be a running joke. Structure does not have one meaning; it has whatever effect the writer built it to have.

words.d: the shape of a story: how its parts are arranged and connected
two story lines told side by side so that each reflects the other
using the same phrase, image or event more than once on purpose
a reporter who sends stories from far away; one of the four men in Crane's boat

lessons.title: Claim and Evidence
lessons.mainIdea: A literary analysis states a claim that could be argued, then supports it with specific evidence from the text.
reading: Here is a sentence that is not a claim: "The Story of an Hour is about a woman whose husband dies." No one could argue with it, so there is nothing to prove. Here is a sentence that is a *claim*: "Chopin makes the reader believe that Louise's death is a loss of freedom, not a shock of joy, even though the doctors say otherwise." Someone could disagree with that. It takes a position on how the story works. A good analysis begins with a sentence like the second one. Every paragraph after it exists to earn it.

The claim must be about the text, not about your feelings. "I liked the ending" is not a claim. "The ending works because the reader knows more than the doctors do" is. Notice that the second sentence names a technique, the gap between what the reader and the doctors know, and links it to an effect. A strong claim often has that shape: the writer does X, which makes the reader Y.

Evidence is what earns the claim. It means specific words and moments from the story, quoted or precisely described. For the claim about Louise, the evidence might include the open window and the spring outside it, the whispered word free, Louise's prayer for a long life, and the fact that the doctors never saw her at the window. Each piece of evidence should be followed by *reasoning*, a sentence or two that explains how this evidence supports the claim. Evidence without reasoning is just a list of quotes.

Try building one paragraph. Start with the claim. Give one piece of evidence, quoted or described exactly. Explain what that evidence shows. Then a second piece, and its explanation. End by saying what the reader now understands. Here is the skeleton written for this lesson: "Chopin sets Louise's discovery in spring. The window is open, the trees are full of new life, and the sky shows blue. These details surround the word free with images of things beginning. When Louise dies an hour later, the reader has been taught to read her death as a life cut off, not a joy too great to bear."

the explanation that connects a piece of evidence to the claim it supports
a specific tool a writer uses, such as pacing, imagery or point of view

lessons.title: Quoting and Explaining
lessons.mainIdea: Quote only the words you need, fit them into your own sentence, and always explain what they show.
reading: A student pastes an entire paragraph of Chopin into her essay and writes underneath it, "This shows Louise is free." The quote is doing nothing, because the reader does not know which words to look at. Now compare: "Chopin does not let Louise shout. She whispers the word 'under her breath,' and the quietness tells us she is discovering something she is not yet allowed to say aloud." Three quoted words, tucked inside the student's own sentence, followed by an explanation. That is how quoting works in an analysis.

Rule one: quote the smallest piece that proves your point. If the striking thing is a single word, quote the word. Rule two: make the quotation part of your own grammar. Instead of dropping a quote on its own line, lead into it: Chopin describes the sky as, or the narrator insists that. This is sometimes called *embedding* a quote. Rule three: after every quotation, write at least one sentence that explains what the words show. Never end a paragraph on a quote, because the last word should be yours.

Here is a model paragraph written for this lesson about the model story of Marcus and the letter. "The story tells us the letter is 'unopened,' and it places that word between two commas, as if the letter itself were set down and left. Marcus goes out to shovel 'for the third time that morning.' A walk does not need to be shoveled three times. The repeated chore is a way of not going back inside, and the reader understands that whatever is in the envelope is something Marcus already knows." Count the quoted words: seven. Count the sentences: four, and each one does work the quotation cannot do on its own.

One more habit. Sometimes you *paraphrase*, meaning you put the text's idea in your own words. Even then, point to where it happens: "When Brently walks in at the end, Chopin gives him an umbrella and travel dust." You have not quoted, but your reader can find the moment. Whether you quote or paraphrase, the job is the same. Show the reader exactly which words on the page carry the weight of your claim. Then carry it yourself.

restating a passage's meaning in your own words while pointing to where it occurs
the exact words of a text, set off with quotation marks

chapters.title: Poetry
chapters.bigQuestion: How can twenty lines of a poem hold more meaning than twenty pages of ordinary prose?

story.title: The Line Everyone Gets Wrong
story.kicker: A poem about a fork in the woods gets printed on posters and read at graduations, and almost nobody notices what it actually says.
paragraphs: In 1916 Robert Frost published a poem that opens with a walker standing where a path splits in two in a yellow autumn wood. He looks down one path as far as he can. He takes the other. The poem's last lines say that he will tell this story someday with a sigh: he took the road less traveled by, and that has made all the difference. You have probably seen those last lines on a coffee mug, a yearbook page or a graduation speech. They sound like a lesson about being brave and different.

Now go back and read the middle of the poem, the part the mugs leave out. The walker says the second road was grassy and wanted wear. Then, in the very next line, he takes it back: as for that, the passing there had worn them really about the same. The stanza after that says both roads lay equally covered in leaves that no step had turned black. In plain words, the two roads were the same. Neither was less traveled. The speaker chose one for no reason he can name.

So why does he say, at the end, that he took the road less traveled? Look at the tense. He is not saying it now. He says he shall be telling this someday, ages and ages hence, with a sigh. He is predicting that his older self will turn a coin flip into a story about courage. Frost said he wrote the poem about a friend who could never decide which path to take on their walks and always sighed afterward about the one he had missed. The poem is a gentle joke about the stories we tell about our own lives.

Frost knew the poem was slippery. Audiences kept hearing it as a hymn to independence, and he once warned that he had to be careful with it. That is the strange thing about a poem. Every word is in plain sight, and readers still see what they expect. The only defense is to read slowly, line by line, and let the poem say what it says instead of what the poster says.

This chapter is about reading that slowly. You will look at how lines are built, how they sound, what pictures they make, who is speaking, where the tone turns, and how the shape of a poem carries its meaning. By the end you will be able to read a poem like the one about the two roads and notice the line everyone else skips.
story.think: Why do you think so many people remember the last two lines of the poem and forget the ones that say the roads were about the same?

lessons.title: Lines and Stanzas
lessons.mainIdea: A poem is built from lines and stanzas, and where a line breaks is a choice that changes how the words are read.
reading: Read these two versions of the same words, written for this lesson. Version one: "My brother left the porch light on for me every night for a year, and then he stopped." Version two: "My brother left the porch light on / for me / every night for a year / and then / he stopped." The words are identical. But in version two your eye pauses at the end of each *line*, and the pauses do something. "For me" sits alone. "And then" hangs in the air before the last two words fall. The slashes mark line breaks, and the breaks are the first thing that makes a poem a poem.

Prose fills the page from margin to margin, and the writer does not control where a line ends. Poetry does. A poet decides where every line stops, and the end of a line is a small silence. Words at the end of a line get extra weight because the reader lands on them. When a sentence spills over the end of one line into the next, it is called *enjambment*, and it pulls the reader forward. When a line ends where the sentence ends, it is *end-stopped*, and it feels settled, like a door closing.

Lines are grouped into *stanzas*, which are the poem's paragraphs. A stanza of two lines is a couplet, of four lines a quatrain. Frost's poem about the two roads has four stanzas of five lines each. Emily Dickinson wrote most of her poems in quatrains. Walt Whitman, in "Song of Myself" from 1855, wrote long, rolling lines with no fixed stanza length at all, and that looseness is part of what he means: a self too large for a tidy box.

When you meet a new poem, count first. How many lines? How many stanzas? Are the lines long or short, even or ragged? Where does the poet break a sentence across a line, and which word ends up alone at the edge? These are not trivia questions. A poem's shape is its first meaning, and you can see it before you understand a single word.

a group of lines in a poem, set off by space, like a paragraph
running a sentence past the end of one line into the next
a line that ends where the sentence or phrase ends, usually with punctuation

lessons.title: Meter and Rhythm
lessons.mainIdea: Meter is a poem's pattern of stressed and unstressed syllables, and the most common English pattern is the ten-syllable line called iambic pentameter.
reading: Say your own name out loud. One syllable is louder than the others: MAR-cus, ta-SHA, jo-SE-fina. English words carry *stress*, and when a poet lines up stressed and unstressed syllables in a repeating pattern, the result is *meter*. Read this line from Shakespeare: "Shall I compare thee to a summer's day?" Tap it out: shall-I com-PARE thee-TO a-SUM mer's-DAY. Soft, loud, soft, loud, five times. That soft-loud pair is called an *iamb*, and five of them in a row make *iambic pentameter*, the line Shakespeare used in his sonnets and most of his plays.

Iambic pentameter is close to the rhythm of ordinary English speech, which is why it can sound natural even when it is strict. Listen to a sentence you might say: "I left my keys inside the other car." Tap it: i-LEFT my-KEYS in-SIDE the-OTH er-CAR. You just spoke a line of iambic pentameter without trying. Poets choose this meter because it gives a line a steady pulse the reader can feel without noticing, like a heartbeat under the words.

Not every poem uses it. Emily Dickinson's poems mostly move in a shorter pattern, lines of eight syllables and six syllables taking turns, the same shape as many hymns. Her poem that begins "Because I could not stop for Death" has that eight-six swing. Walt Whitman threw meter out and wrote in *free verse*, lines with no fixed count, held together by repetition and breath instead of a beat. Each choice makes a different music, and the music is part of the meaning.

The best way to hear meter is to read aloud and exaggerate. Overdo the loud syllables. Then notice where a line breaks the pattern. When a poem has kept a steady beat for ten lines and suddenly stumbles, the poet almost always did it on purpose, and the stumble is pointing at something. Meter is not a test to pass. It is a rhythm to feel, and then a place to look for the moment the rhythm changes.

lessons.title: Sound Devices
lessons.mainIdea: Poets repeat sounds on purpose, through rhyme, alliteration and assonance, so that the ear connects words the mind might not.
reading: Read this line written for this lesson: "The bus was late, and the light was low, and the boys at the back were bored." Say it aloud. Hear the b sounds bumping along: bus, back, boys, bored. That repeated first sound is *alliteration*. Now hear the long o inside light, low and boys, and the long a in late. Repeated vowel sounds inside words are *assonance*. None of these are accidents. A poet, or any careful writer, uses sound to tie words together and to give a line a texture you can feel in your mouth.

The best-known sound device is *rhyme*, matching the ending sounds of words, usually at the ends of lines. Frost's stanzas about the two roads rhyme in a pattern: the first, third and fourth lines share one sound, the second and fifth another. That pattern is written as ABAAB, using letters for each sound. A rhyme scheme is a kind of promise. Once the reader hears the first A, the ear waits for the second, and the poet can satisfy that wait or play with it.

Rhyme can also be imperfect. Dickinson often ends lines with words that almost rhyme and do not quite, like soul and all. This is called *slant rhyme*. It makes the ear lean in, expecting a match and getting something slightly off, which suits a poet who liked to tell the truth at an angle. Paul Laurence Dunbar, writing in the 1890s, used full rhyme and strong rhythm in "We Wear the Mask," and the polished sound is part of the point: the mask is smooth, and the pain is underneath.

To find sound devices, read the poem aloud twice. The first time, just listen. The second time, mark every sound you hear more than once in a line or two: a consonant at the start of words, a vowel inside them, a rhyme at the end. Then ask which words the sound has linked. If bored and boys are tied by a b, the poem has quietly put the boys' boredom into the sound of the line itself.

repeating a vowel sound inside nearby words: light, low, boys
matching ending sounds, usually at the ends of lines
a near rhyme, where the sounds almost but do not fully match, such as soul and all

lessons.title: Imagery
lessons.mainIdea: Imagery is language that makes the reader see, hear, smell, taste or touch something, and it is the poem's main way of making feeling physical.
reading: Compare two lines written for this lesson. "I was nervous before the test." And: "The pencil left a wet print on my thumb." The first line names a feeling. The second gives you a thumb, a pencil and sweat, and the feeling arrives on its own. That is *imagery*: words that appeal to the five senses. Most beginning readers think imagery means pretty description. It does not. It means concrete, physical detail that lets the reader's body understand what the speaker's body felt.

Look at the opening of Frost's poem about the two roads: a yellow wood. Not a forest, not autumn, just the color. It puts you in a specific light. Later he says the leaves that morning had not been trodden black, which makes you see fresh yellow leaves and imagine the dark stain a footprint leaves on wet ones. Frost's later poem "Stopping by Woods on a Snowy Evening," from 1923, is almost nothing but imagery: a horse shaking its harness bells, the only other sound the sweep of easy wind and downy flake.

Imagery works because the senses do not argue. If a poem tells you a character is sad, you may or may not believe it. If a poem shows a plate of food going cold on a table set for two, you feel the sadness before you name it. Dickinson describes hope as a bird that perches in the soul and sings a tune without words. You cannot see hope. You can see a small bird, and the poem lets the bird carry the idea.

When you read a poem, mark every word that hits a sense. Circle colors, sounds, textures, smells and tastes. Then ask what feeling those images add up to, and notice that the poem probably never named the feeling directly. When you write about imagery, do not just list the images. Say what each one makes the reader sense and what that sensation makes the reader understand.

specific and physical, something you could point to, rather than abstract
an idea that cannot be seen or touched, such as hope or sadness

lessons.title: Figurative Language
lessons.mainIdea: Metaphor, simile and personification say one thing is another, or is like another, so that the reader understands both differently.
reading: Robert Burns wrote in 1794 that his love was like a red, red rose newly sprung in June. He did not mean she had thorns. He meant that something about her was fresh, bright and new, and he trusted the reader to carry those qualities from the rose to the woman. That comparison, using like or as, is a *simile*. Take away the like and say the thing directly, "my love is a rose," and it becomes a *metaphor*. Both are *figurative language*: words that mean something other than their plain, literal sense.

Dickinson's hope is a metaphor. She does not say hope is like a bird; she says it is the thing with feathers. Shakespeare's most famous sonnet opens by asking whether he should compare someone to a summer's day, and then spends the poem finding all the ways the person is better than summer. In his sonnet that begins by saying his mistress's eyes are nothing like the sun, he mocks the whole habit of comparison. He lists all the flattering similes other poets use and denies each one, then says at the end that his love is as rare as any woman who has been praised with false comparisons.

A third kind of figure gives human actions or feelings to something that is not human. Dickinson's poem about a carriage ride describes Death as a polite driver who kindly stopped for her. That is *personification*. Death has no manners, but the poem gives him some, and the effect is chilling in a quiet way. Here is a model written for this lesson: "The radiator in my grandmother's apartment complained all winter and then, in April, gave up." A radiator cannot complain or give up. The words make it a tired old companion, which is what the speaker is really describing.

When you find a figure of speech, do two things. First, name the two things being connected: love and a rose, hope and a bird, death and a driver. Second, ask which qualities cross over and which do not. The poet chose the comparison for some qualities, and the reader's job is to find those and leave the rest. Nobody thinks the beloved has thorns. Everybody understands June.

words.d: words used to mean something beyond their literal sense
a comparison using like or as: my love is like a red rose
a comparison that says one thing is another: hope is the thing with feathers
giving human traits to something not human: a radiator that complains

lessons.title: The Speaker Is Not the Poet
lessons.mainIdea: The voice in a poem is a speaker the poet created, and the two may agree, disagree or be worlds apart.
reading: Read this poem written for this lesson: "I have been driving this truck for thirty years / and I have never once looked in the mirror / to see what I left behind." A student reading it might say that the poet has been a truck driver for thirty years. But the poet might be nineteen. The poet might take the bus. The I in a poem is the *speaker*, a voice the poet builds the way a fiction writer builds a narrator. Sometimes the speaker is very close to the poet. Sometimes the speaker is a character the poet would never want to be.

Robert Browning's poem "My Last Duchess," from 1842, is spoken by a duke showing a visitor a painting of his dead wife. He complains that she smiled at everyone, not only at him, and he hints, calmly, that he gave orders and the smiles stopped. Browning was not a murderer. He built a speaker who reveals himself as one without meaning to, and the reader's horror comes from hearing the duke's polished voice say what he does not know he is saying.

Even when the speaker seems to be the poet, keep the distinction. Whitman's "Song of Myself" begins by celebrating himself and says that every atom belonging to him belongs to the reader too. That I is enormous, containing crowds and continents. Whitman the man lived in Brooklyn and worked as a printer and nurse. The I of the poem is a made thing, and treating it as the poet's diary shrinks it. Dunbar's mask poem says we, and the we is African Americans facing a country that demanded a smile. Dunbar shaped that voice deliberately, choosing the plural to speak for many.

So when you write about a poem, say the speaker, not the poet, unless the poem clearly names the author or the poet has said the poem is about their own life. Then ask what kind of speaker the poet built. What does this voice know, want, hide or fail to see? In the truck poem, the speaker says he never looked back. The poem is only three lines long, and all of them are about looking back. The speaker does not notice that. The poet does, and so should you.

a poem spoken by a character to a listener, revealing the character's nature, as in My Last Duchess
a voice or character a poet adopts that is not simply the poet's own

lessons.title: Hearing the Tone
lessons.mainIdea: Tone is the speaker's attitude toward the subject, and you hear it in word choice, rhythm and what is left unsaid.
reading: Your friend texts "great" after you tell her the plan. Is she pleased, or is she rolling her eyes? You cannot tell from the one word. You need the context, the timing, whether she used a period. In a poem, that attitude is the *tone*, and finding it is one of the hardest and most important parts of reading. Tone is not what the poem is about. It is how the speaker feels about what it is about: tender, bitter, amused, grieving, mocking, calm.

You hear tone in diction first. Read this pair written for this lesson. "My father's chair still sits beside the stove." And: "My father's chair is still taking up space by the stove." Same chair, same stove. The first is quiet and sad; still sits is gentle. The second is irritated; taking up space treats the chair as an obstacle, and maybe the father too. The tone lives in three words. Change them and the whole poem changes.

Tone also lives in rhythm and in restraint. Dickinson's carriage poem describes Death, a grave and eternity, in a steady hymn rhythm with almost no drama. The calmness is the tone, and it is unsettling precisely because the subject is not calm. Frost's poem about fire and ice, from 1920, takes the end of the world and handles it with a shrug: some say fire, some say ice, and the speaker allows that either would do. The offhand tone about the largest possible subject is the joke and the chill at once.

To name a tone, avoid the vague words first: happy, sad, serious. Push for something exact: wistful, defiant, weary, tender, sardonic. Then prove it. Point to the two or three words that carry the attitude, and to the rhythm, and to anything the speaker refuses to say. Two readers may hear different tones in the same lines. That is fine, as long as each can point to the words that made them hear it.

holding back emotion or drama in the words, which can itself create tone
gently sad and longing for something past or out of reach

lessons.title: The Turn
lessons.mainIdea: Many poems pivot at a certain line, changing tone, direction or meaning, and finding that turn is the key to reading the poem.
reading: Shakespeare's sonnet about the summer's day spends eight lines on what is wrong with summer: it is too short, too hot, too cloudy, and it fades. Then line nine begins with the word but. From there the poem changes direction. The beloved's summer will not fade, because the poem itself will keep it alive as long as people can read. That pivot is the *turn*, sometimes called by its Italian name, the *volta*. Nearly every sonnet has one, and learning to spot it is like finding the hinge of a door.

A sonnet is fourteen lines of iambic pentameter. The kind Shakespeare wrote has three quatrains and a final couplet, and the couplet often delivers the turn or a last twist after it. In the sonnet that mocks flattering comparisons, twelve lines deny that the mistress is like the sun, coral, snow, roses or music. Then the couplet turns: and yet, the speaker says, his love is as rare as any woman ever praised with false comparisons. The insult was a setup. The turn reveals the real tenderness underneath.

Turns are not only for sonnets. Dunbar's mask poem describes the grin and the lie for a stanza, then turns to a cry: why should the world be wise about our pain? Frost's two roads poem turns at the last stanza, when the speaker leaps into the future and starts telling the story his older self will tell. Here is a model written for this lesson: "I said I did not need the ride. / I said it twice, and meant it once. / You drove off slow enough to let me change my mind." The turn is the last line, where the speaker's stubbornness meets someone else's patience.

To find the turn, look for signal words: but, yet, and yet, still, then, now. Look for a change in tense, from past to future, or in address, from talking about someone to talking to them. Look for the place where the tone shifts, where a mocking voice softens or a calm voice cracks. Then ask what the poem means after the turn that it did not mean before. Often the whole poem was built to reach that line.

a fourteen-line poem in iambic pentameter, usually with a turn

lessons.title: Structure Makes Meaning
lessons.mainIdea: The shape of a poem, its stanzas, repetitions and ending, is not a container for the meaning; it is part of the meaning.
reading: Go back to Frost's poem about the two roads and look at where things fall. Stanza one: the fork. Stanza two: the choice, and the admission that the roads were about the same. Stanza three: both roads lay equal that morning, and the speaker doubts he will ever come back. Stanza four: the future story, told with a sigh. The poem's *structure* walks the reader from an honest present into a dishonest future, one stanza at a time. The four identical stanzas march the reader forward while the speaker, in the last one, starts rewriting the walk.

Frost's snowy woods poem does something similar with its ending. Three stanzas describe stopping, the horse, the quiet snow. The last stanza says the woods are lovely, dark and deep, but the speaker has promises to keep and miles to go before he sleeps. Then it says the last line again. Word for word. The *repetition* of that line is the whole poem's weight. The first time, it is about a journey. The second time, because it is repeated and the poem stops there, sleep starts to sound like something larger, and the speaker seems to be talking himself out of staying in the dark.

Structure includes what a poet does with length. A short poem that ends abruptly can feel like a door slammed. A poem that circles back to its opening image can feel like a life closing. Here is a model written for this lesson: "Monday, the phone. / Tuesday, the phone. / Wednesday, the phone, and I let it ring. / Thursday, nothing." Four lines, one per day, and the meaning is entirely in the pattern: repetition, a small act of refusal, then silence, which is worse.

When you write about structure, describe the shape before you interpret it. How many parts? What does each part do? Where does the poem repeat, and where does it break the pattern? Then say what the shape makes the reader feel that the words alone would not. Frost could have written a paragraph saying that people invent brave stories about arbitrary choices. Instead he built four stanzas that let the reader watch it happen.

saying a word, phrase or line more than once so that it gains weight
made for no particular reason, such as choosing between two identical roads

lessons.title: Paraphrase First
lessons.mainIdea: Before you analyze a poem, put it into plain prose in your own words so that you know what it literally says.
reading: Students often jump from reading a poem to writing about its deep meaning in a single step. The writing wobbles, because the first step was skipped. The first step is *paraphrase*: restating the poem, line by line or stanza by stanza, in your own ordinary sentences, with nothing added. A paraphrase of Frost's last stanza might be: "Years from now, I will tell people, with a sigh, that when the road split I took the one fewer people used, and that this changed everything." That is all the stanza says. The analysis comes after.

Paraphrasing forces you to solve the poem's puzzles instead of stepping around them. What does thou ow'st mean in Shakespeare's line about eternal summer? You have to find out that ow'st means own or possess before you can paraphrase it: your beauty will not lose what it has. Old words, inverted sentences and dropped subjects all get untangled when you have to say the line plainly. If you cannot paraphrase a line, you do not yet know what it says, and you are not ready to say what it means.

Here is a stanza written for this lesson, followed by a paraphrase. Poem: "My mother kept the receipt for everything, / a shoebox of proof that we had paid, / as if the world might someday ask." Paraphrase: "The speaker's mother saved every receipt in a shoebox, as evidence that the family had paid for things, because she seemed to fear that someone might one day demand proof." Notice the paraphrase is longer than the poem. That is normal. Poems compress; prose unpacks.

A paraphrase is not an analysis, and you should not hand it in as one. But you should write it, keep it, and read it next to the poem. The gap between the two is where the poem's art is. The paraphrase says the mother saved receipts. The poem says a shoebox of proof and as if the world might someday ask. Everything in that gap, the box, the fear, the tone, is what your paragraph will be about.

words.d: restating a text in your own plain words without adding interpretation
to pack a lot of meaning into few words, as poems do
in reversed word order, such as a verb placed before its subject

Because poems compress meaning and prose unpacks it
Because paraphrases must include the title
check.why: Poems pack meaning tightly; saying the same thing plainly takes more words.

check.q: What does the gap between a poem and its paraphrase show you?
choices: That the paraphrase is wrong
That poems are impossible to understand
That the poem should have been written in prose
Where the poem's art lives, in the words the plain version cannot carry
check.why: The images and tones lost in paraphrase are exactly what an analysis should discuss.

lessons.title: Writing About a Poem
lessons.mainIdea: A strong paragraph about a poem makes one claim about how the poem works, quotes the exact words that show it, and explains the effect.
reading: A paragraph about a poem has the same bones as a paragraph about a story. Claim, evidence, reasoning. The difference is that a poem's evidence is smaller and denser. A single word, a line break, a repeated sound can carry the argument. Here is a claim written for this lesson: "In Frost's poem about the two roads, the last stanza does not celebrate a brave choice; it shows the speaker preparing to tell a flattering story about a choice that made no difference." That claim could be argued against, which is what makes it a claim.

Now the evidence. Quote the poem's own admission that the roads had been worn really about the same, and point out that this line comes before the famous ending. Quote the future tense, I shall be telling this, and the phrase ages and ages hence. Quote the sigh. Each piece of evidence gets a sentence of reasoning: the sigh could be regret or satisfaction, and the poem refuses to say which; the future tense means the speaker is predicting a story, not reporting a fact. Keep quotations short and set them inside your own sentences.

Here is a full model paragraph written for this lesson about the receipt poem. "The speaker's mother is not simply organized; she is afraid. The poem calls her shoebox 'proof that we had paid,' and proof is a word for courtrooms, not kitchens. The last line, 'as if the world might someday ask,' turns the world into an accuser waiting at the door. The line break before 'as if' leaves the receipts hanging for a moment, and then the fear arrives. By the end, a box of paper has become a defense against a world the mother does not trust." Claim, three pieces of evidence, reasoning for each, and a closing sentence in the writer's own words.

Before you hand in a paragraph about a poem, check four things. Does the first sentence make a claim someone could dispute? Does every quotation stay under a line and sit inside your sentence? Does each quotation get at least one sentence explaining its effect? Does the paragraph say speaker and not poet? If all four are yes, you have written literary analysis, and you have done it with a form most people are afraid of.

words.d: a statement about how a poem works that a reader could argue against
the exact words, sounds or line breaks from the poem that support a claim
the explanation of how a piece of evidence produces an effect and supports the claim
